docs.title: Robot-Joint Actuator FOC Testbed
docs.text:
One robot joint built the way humanoid and legged-robot actuators are built: a brushless motor, a magnetic encoder, field-oriented control on an STM32G4, model-based fault detection and a CAN link to a Python test stack.

Simulation-first: every loop is designed and tuned in a plant model, implemented in hardware-independent C, and tested against the model before it drives a motor.

STM32G474FOCC99CANAS5047PPythonSIL testing

See the results How it works View source files

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Humanoid and legged robots are built from compact joint actuators: a brushless motor, a reduction, an encoder and a driver running field-oriented control (FOC) tens of thousands of times a second. This testbed is one of those joints, built to study how well it can be controlled and how quickly it can tell when something goes wrong.

The stack has three layers that share one design:

Layer What it does Simulation (sim/) Surface-PMSM plant with sensor models, cascaded FOC controller, fault monitor and 8 experiments that regenerate every figure on this site Firmware (firmware/) Hardware-independent C99 core (FOC math, cascade, fault detectors, CAN protocol, AS5047P driver) plus STM32G474 HAL glue; unit tests and software-in-the-loop against the plant model Host (host/) python-can link with a 1 kHz logger, test profiles, encoder calibration, sim-vs-hardware comparison and a virtual joint that speaks the real protocol 
flowchart LR
  subgraph Joint
    M[BLDC / PMSM motor] --- E[AS5047P magnetic encoder]
    D[STM32G474 FOC driver] -->|PWM| M
    E -->|SPI angle| D
  end
  D <-->|CAN| H[Python host: logger, tests, calibration]
  S[Plant model + controller sim] -. same algorithm, SIL tests .-> D

docs.title: CAN protocol
docs.text:
Classic CAN, 1 Mbit/s, 8 data bytes, little-endian. 11-bit identifier:

ID = (msg << 4) | node_id        node_id 0..15, msg 0x00..0x7F

Source of truth: firmware/core/inc/can_protocol.h (C) and host/actuator_host/protocol.py (Python). host/tests/test_protocol.py and firmware/tests/test_main.c check the same byte layout.

docs.title: Host to joint
docs.text:
msg Name Payload Notes 0x01 SET_MODE u8 mode 0 idle, 1 torque, 2 velocity, 3 position (holds current angle), 4 current 0x02 SET_TORQUE f32 torque [Nm] iq = tau / Kt, clamped to I_max 0x03 SET_VELOCITY f32 vel [rad/s], f32 torque_ff [Nm] 0x04 SET_POSITION f32 pos [rad], i16 vel_ff [0.01 rad/s], i16 torque_ff [mNm] stream at 200-1000 Hz for trajectories 0x05 SET_CURRENT f32 iq [A], f32 id [A] loop tests only 0x06 CLEAR_FAULTS - returns to IDLE 0x07 ESTOP - IDLE immediately 0x08 SET_PARAM u8 param, 3 pad, f32 value only in IDLE; re-derives all gains 0x09 HOST_HEARTBEAT - any host frame resets the 50 ms comms watchdog 0x0A CALIBRATE f32 electrical angle [rad], f32 current [A] open-loop alignment for encoder offset

SET_PARAM ids: 1 current bandwidth [Hz], 2 velocity bandwidth, 3 position bandwidth, 4 collision threshold [Nm], 5 encoder electrical offset [rad], 6 current limit [A].

docs.title: Joint to host
docs.text:
msg Name Rate Payload 0x10 STATUS 100 Hz u8 mode, i8 winding temp estimate [C], u16 fault bits, u32 time [us] 0x11 TELEM_STATE 1 kHz f32 position [rad], f32 velocity [rad/s] 0x12 TELEM_CURRENT 1 kHz i16 iq [mA], i16 iq_ref [mA], i16 id [mA], u16 vbus [10 mV] 0x13 TELEM_OBS 1 kHz i16 observer external torque [mNm], u16 voltage residual [mV], u32 time [us]

Bus load: 3 telemetry frames x 1 kHz x ~130 bits = ~39 % of 1 Mbit/s for one joint, plus commands. For more joints, drop telemetry to 500 Hz or move to CAN-FD (the G474 supports it; the CANable 2.0 does too with the right firmware).

docs.title: Fault bits
docs.text: Bit Fault Detector 0 OVERCURRENT any phase above 4 A (instantaneous) 1 OVERTEMP lumped thermal model with copper tempco, 90 C 2 UNDERVOLT bus below 18 V 3 ENC_FLAG AS5047 parity or error flag 4 ENC_JUMP angle change above 0.05 rad in one 50 us tick 5 ENC_MODEL back-EMF voltage residual above 1.2 V for 2 ms (silent encoder fault) 6 FOLLOWING position error above 0.35 rad 7 COLLISION momentum-observer external torque above 0.08 Nm 8 COMM_TIMEOUT no host frame for 50 ms while active

• Simulation: surface-PMSM plant with sensor models, cascaded FOC controller, fault monitor, 8 experiments, demo video renderer, regression tests.
  • Firmware core (C99): FOC math, cascade, back-EMF residual and momentum-observer fault detection, CAN protocol, AS5047P driver, encoder calibration mode. Host unit tests and software-in-the-loop.
  • STM32G474 + IHM07M1 HAL glue and CubeMX settings.
  • Host tools: python-can link with a 1 kHz logger, test profiles, encoder calibration, sim-vs-hardware comparison, and a virtual joint on the real protocol.
  • Documentation: getting started, design and theory, CAN protocol, system identification, research ideas.
  • CI: GitHub Actions runs the Python and firmware tests and regenerates the figures.

docs.title: 60-90 s demo video shot list
docs.text:
1. (5 s) Hardware overview: motor, encoder, Nucleo + driver, CANable, e-stop. Title card.
  2. (10 s) Screen split: sim step response vs hardware step response overlaid (compare_sim).
  3. (10 s) Position steps and sine tracking, live plot next to the moving inertia disk.
  4. (10 s) Feedforward on/off: tracking error drops (show the RMS number).
  5. (15 s) Collision demo: joint swings into a foam block, stops on contact; plot shows the observer spike.
  6. (15 s) Encoder fault demo: pull the encoder connector (or trigger the injected freeze) while spinning; joint stops, STATUS shows ENC_MODEL.
  7. (5 s) Comms watchdog: kill the Python script, joint goes safe.
  8. (5 s) End card: repo link, one line on what is next (fault-tolerant control).

Film at 60 fps with the plot on a second monitor, or capture the screen and the bench separately and edit side by side.

docs.title: Design and theory
docs.text: This document explains why the controller looks the way it does. Every number here comes from sim/actuator_sim/params.py and is reproduced by python -m experiments.run_all.

docs.title: 1. Plant model
docs.text:
A surface-mounted PMSM (gimbal and most outrunner robot motors) has equal d and q inductance, so in the rotor frame:

L \frac{di_d}{dt} = v_d - R i_d + \omega_e L i_q
L \frac{di_q}{dt} = v_q - R i_q - \omega_e L i_d - \omega_e \lambda
\tau_m = \tfrac{3}{2} p \lambda i_q = K_t i_q
J \dot\omega = \tau_m - b\omega - T_c \,\mathrm{sgn}(\omega) + \tau_{ext}

with p pole pairs, electrical speed ω_e = p·ω and flux linkage λ = K_t / (1.5 p). Torque depends only on i_q, so FOC holds i_d = 0 and controls torque through i_q.

The simulation integrates this at 5 substeps per 50 µs PWM period. Voltages are applied in the stationary (α, β) frame and held over each period (average-value inverter), so rotor motion inside a period and any controller angle error are captured physically, not approximated. The controller output computed at sample k is applied during period k+1 (one-period compute delay), as on the STM32.

Sensor models: 14-bit absolute encoder (AS5047P), phase current noise of 10 mA rms plus 12-bit ADC quantisation.

docs.title: 2. Current loop (20 kHz)
docs.text:
The plant from v_q to i_q (after decoupling) is first order:

G_i(s) = \frac{1}{Ls + R}

A PI with Kp = L·ω_c and Ki = R·ω_c puts its zero on the plant pole, so the loop gain is ω_c / s and the closed loop is first order with bandwidth ω_c. The design uses f_c = 1 kHz. The 1.5-sample delay (compute + PWM) costs ω_c · 1.5 T_s = 27°, leaving a 63° phase margin (07_open_loop_bode.png). 1.5 kHz was tried first and gave 49° margin and 19 % overshoot, so it was lowered.

Additions on top of the PI:

  • Decoupling and back-EMF feedforward: v_d gets -ω_e L i_q, v_q gets ω_e L i_d + ω_e λ, so the PI only fights model error.
  • Angle advance: the inverse Park uses θ_e + 1.5 T_s ω_e, so the voltage lands where the rotor will be when the PWM applies it.
  • Circular voltage limit with d priority: |v| ≤ V_bus/√3 (the linear SVPWM range); q gets what d leaves.
  • Conditional-integration anti-windup: the integrator stops when the output is saturated and the error pushes further into saturation.

Note on large steps: with Kp = 14 V/A, a 1 A step asks for more voltage than the 13.9 V the inverter can make, so the response becomes slew-limited by V_bus. The step test uses 0.5 A to measure the linear loop.

docs.title: 3. Velocity loop (5 kHz) and the PLL
docs.text:
The encoder difference over one 200 µs velocity period is quantised to 2π/16384 / 200 µs ≈ 1.9 rad/s, which is too noisy for a fast loop. A type-2 phase-locked loop tracks the multi-turn angle and gives a smooth velocity:

e = \theta_{meas} - \hat\theta, \quad \dot{\hat\omega} = k_i e, \quad \dot{\hat\theta} = \hat\omega + k_p e

with k_p = 2ω_n, k_i = ω_n² (ζ = 1) and f_n = 400 Hz.

With the current loop much faster, the velocity plant is K_t / (J s). A PI with Kp = J ω_v / K_t crosses over at ω_v (f_v = 80 Hz) and the integral corner sits at ω_v / 5, giving 68° phase margin. Torque feedforward enters as τ_ff / K_t.

docs.title: 4. Position loop (1 kHz)
docs.text:
Near the target the loop is a P controller with Kp = ω_p (12 Hz), giving a velocity command. For a large step a linear P asks for full speed until the last moment, and the current limit cannot brake in time, which caused 11-13 % overshoot. The fix is a braking curve: the velocity command is the smaller of the linear law and the speed from which the joint can still stop,

v_{cmd} = \mathrm{sgn}(e)\,\min\left(K_p |e|,\ \sqrt{2 a_{max} |e|}\right), \quad a_{max} = 0.7\,K_t I_{max} / J

which removes the overshoot (90° step: 0 %, 67 ms settle). For trajectories the host also sends velocity and torque feedforward (J q̈ + b q̇ + T_c sgn q̇). That takes 2 Hz sine tracking error from 6.6° to 0.037° RMS.

docs.title: 5. Fault detection
docs.text: Detector Signal Catches Ignores Over-current max phase current > 4 A shorts, runaway - Encoder flag / jump AS5047 parity, error bit, Δθ > 0.05 rad per tick wiring and SPI faults silent freezes Back-EMF residual applied voltage minus R i + L di/dt + ω_e L J i + ω_e λ silent encoder freeze, magnet slip, wrong offset load torque, collisions Momentum observer estimated external torque collisions, jams, unexpected loads sensor faults (while the encoder is healthy) Following error position error > 0.35 rad gross failures fast, small contacts Thermal model I²R with copper tempco into a first-order thermal mass overheating - Comms watchdog no host frame for 50 ms crashed PC, unplugged CAN -

docs.title: Back-EMF (voltage-model) residual
docs.text:
The voltage applied over the last PWM period, rotated into the mid-period measured frame, must equal what the model predicts from the measured currents and the measured speed:

r = v_{applied} - \left(R\,\bar i + L\,\frac{\Delta i}{T_s} + \hat\omega_e L J \bar i + \hat\omega_e \lambda\,\hat q\right)

If the encoder freezes while the rotor turns, ω̂_e drops to zero but the real back-EMF does not, so |r| jumps to about ω_e λ. External torque changes the current but not this voltage balance, so the residual separates sensor faults from mechanical events. Two implementation details mattered:

  • Filtering |r| directly rectified current-sense noise into a 0.8 V bias. Filtering the vector (r_d, r_q) at 150 Hz first and then taking the magnitude dropped the normal level to about 0.03 V.
  • The applied voltage must be expressed in the frame at the middle of the period it was applied in, not in the delay-compensated frame it was computed in.

Threshold 1.2 V held for 2 ms: the largest normal value seen in aggressive current-limited moves is 0.87 V; a freeze at 20 rad/s reaches about 3 V. Detection takes 3.3 ms in both the Python model and the C firmware.

docs.title: Generalised momentum observer
docs.text:
r(t) = K\left(J\hat\omega(t) - J\hat\omega(0) - \int_0^t \left(\tau_m - b\hat\omega - T_c\,\mathrm{sgn}\,\hat\omega + r\right) d\tau\right)

r follows the external torque through a first-order filter of bandwidth K (60 Hz) without differentiating velocity. Because the PLL velocity lags the true velocity by about k_p/k_i during acceleration, a current-limited velocity step produced a 0.09 Nm false reading. Lagging τ_m by 1.5 k_p/k_i (tuned in sim) cut that to 0.018 Nm, under the 0.08 Nm collision threshold. Result: contact is detected 0.8 ms after it starts, and peak contact torque is 0.12 Nm, against 30 ms and 0.45 Nm for a following-error check.

docs.title: 6. Simulation to firmware
docs.text: firmware/core/src/actuator.c is a line-for-line port of sim/actuator_sim/control.py + faults.py. The firmware test (make -C firmware/tests) runs the C controller against a C copy of the plant and must reproduce the sim: 30.02 rad/s on a 30 rad/s step, 1.5712 rad on a 90° step, encoder freeze caught in 3.3 ms. When you change one side, change the other and run both test suites.

docs.title: 7. Known limitations
docs.text:
• Motor parameters are estimates until bench identification.
  • Single-precision multi-turn angle loses resolution after many turns (about 7 µrad at 100 rad). It is fine for a joint with limited travel. A continuous-rotation wheel would need an integer turn counter.
  • No field weakening, cogging compensation or dead-time compensation yet. The L6230 handles dead time internally.
  • Trajectories streamed from a PC show timing jitter. The over-CAN virtual test gave 3.6° RMS tracking error against 0.037° in pure sim. Next step: an on-board trajectory generator.

docs.title: Firmware (STM32G474 + IHM07M1)
docs.text:
firmware/
  core/            hardware-independent C99: FOC math, cascade, faults, CAN protocol, AS5047
  app/main_stm32.c HAL glue: ISR wiring, CAN, startup calibration (paste into a CubeIDE project)
  tests/           host build of core/ + unit tests + software-in-the-loop run

core/ is the same algorithm as sim/actuator_sim/ (gains, anti-windup, PLL, back-EMF residual, momentum observer). Run the host tests after every change:

make -C firmware/tests      # builds with -Werror -Wdouble-promotion, runs unit + SIL tests

The SIL test closes the loop between the real actuator.c and a C port of the plant model and checks a velocity step, a 90 deg position step and silent encoder-freeze detection.

docs.title: CubeMX setup (NUCLEO-G474RE)
docs.text:
Peripheral Setting SYSCLK 170 MHz (HSE 24 MHz from ST-Link MCO or HSI + PLL) TIM1 Center-aligned mode 1, ARR = 4250 (20 kHz at 170 MHz), CH1/2/3 PWM (IHM07M1 IN1/2/3), CH4 PWM at ARR-1 as TRGO2 for ADC, dead time not needed (L6230 handles it), break input to the e-stop line ADC1 / ADC2 Injected group triggered by TIM1 TRGO2; ADC1 rank1 = phase A shunt, rank2 = VBUS; ADC2 rank1 = phase B shunt; sample time ~ 24.5 cycles SPI1 Mode 1 (CPOL 0, CPHA 1), 16-bit, 5-10 MHz, software CS on a GPIO named ENC_CS FDCAN1 Classic CAN, 1 Mbit/s (prescaler/segments from the CubeMX calculator, sample point ~ 80 %), pins PA11/PA12 to SN65HVD230 TIM6 1 kHz update interrupt GPIO DRV_EN (L6230 EN1/2/3 tied), ENC_CS, NTC on a spare ADC channel NVIC priorities ADC injected (0, highest) > FDCAN (2) > TIM6 (3)

Check the IHM07M1 user manual for the exact shunt pins and op-amp gain; the ADC_TO_AMPS constant in main_stm32.c is a starting value to calibrate against a bench multimeter.

docs.title: Bring-up order (do not skip)
docs.text:
1. Bench supply at 12 V, 0.5 A limit. Run with MODE_IDLE and check telemetry: angle tracks hand rotation, currents read ~0.
  2. Encoder direction and electrical offset: host/scripts/calibrate_encoder.py (holds a d-axis current vector, reads the angle, computes enc_offset_e, checks direction).
  3. Current loop alone (MODE_CURRENT) with the rotor clamped. Compare the step to sim/figures/01_current_step.png.
  4. Velocity loop, then position loop. Raise the supply limit only after each loop matches the sim.
  5. Fault tests: unplug the encoder connector while spinning slowly, stop the host program (comms timeout), grab the inertia disk (collision).

docs.title: CPU budget (estimate, check with a GPIO toggle + scope)
docs.text: At 170 MHz the 20 kHz ISR has 8500 cycles. Expected cost: ~300 cycles for the current loop with sinf/cosf from newlib (replace with CMSIS-DSP arm_sin_cos_f32 or the CORDIC peripheral if needed), ~400 for the residual and observer, ~600 for the SPI read at 10 MHz. Budget leaves >80 % headroom.

docs.title: 1. Install (Windows, macOS or Linux)
docs.text:
Python 3.10 or newer and a C compiler (for the firmware tests) are all you need.

git clone https://github.com/<you>/actuator-foc-testbed.git
cd actuator-foc-testbed
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate            # Windows   (macOS/Linux: source .venv/bin/activate)
pip install -e ".[dev]"

On Windows the firmware tests need gcc and make. MSYS2 (pacman -S mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-gcc make) or WSL both work. STM32CubeIDE also ships a GCC, but it is the ARM cross-compiler and cannot build the host tests.

docs.title: 2. Check everything works (no hardware)
docs.text:
pytest -q                                   # 13 tests: sim, protocol, virtual joint over CAN
make -C firmware/tests                      # C unit tests + software-in-the-loop
cd sim
python -m experiments.run_all               # 8 figures + figures/results.json  (~10 s)
python -m experiments.make_video            # figures/actuator_sim_demo.mp4/.gif (~1 min, needs ffmpeg)

Expected output of the firmware tests:

SIL: velocity 30.017 rad/s, position 1.5712 rad (peak 1.5712), encoder fault 0x20 after 3.3 ms
all firmware core tests passed

docs.title: 3. Explore with the virtual joint
docs.text:
The virtual joint runs the simulation behind the real CAN protocol, so the host tools behave exactly as they will with hardware:

python host/scripts/run_test.py --interface virtual --test velocity_step
python host/scripts/run_test.py --interface virtual --test position_step
python host/scripts/run_test.py --interface virtual --test sine_tracking
python host/scripts/run_test.py --interface virtual --test comm_timeout

Each run writes logs/<time>_<test>.csv, .png and .json (metrics).

To run the joint as a separate process, like a real device:

pip install msgpack                                   # needed by python-can's udp_multicast bus
python -m actuator_host.virtual_joint                 # terminal 1
python host/scripts/run_test.py --interface udp_multicast --channel 239.0.0.1 --test velocity_step   # terminal 2

Fault injection on the virtual joint: --encoder-freeze-at 2.0 (seconds) or --wall-at 0.6 (radians).

docs.title: 4. Change the design
docs.text: You want to Edit Then Use measured motor values MotorParams in sim/actuator_sim/params.py and act_default_config in firmware/core/src/actuator.c rerun sim + firmware tests Change loop bandwidths Bandwidths (sim) and bw_* (firmware); gains re-derive automatically check 07_open_loop_bode.png margins Tune fault thresholds FaultThresholds (sim) and the *_trip, bemf_*, collision_nm fields (firmware) check no false trips: pytest -q Add a CAN message firmware/core/inc/can_protocol.h + .c, host/actuator_host/protocol.py, docs/can_protocol.md add a byte-layout test on both sides

docs.title: 5. Hardware wiring (NUCLEO-G474RE + X-NUCLEO-IHM07M1)
docs.text:
Connection From To Driver IHM07M1 stacked on the Nucleo Arduino/Morpho headers jumpers per IHM07M1 manual for 3-shunt sensing Motor phases GM4108 three wires IHM07M1 OUT1/2/3 (order only sets direction; calibration detects it) DC bus Bench supply 24 V, current limit 1 A to start inline fuse, then e-stop (normally closed), then IHM07M1 VIN Encoder AS5047P breakout, 3.3 V SPI1: SCK PA5, MISO PA6, MOSI PA7, CS any free GPIO named ENC_CS Magnet diametric 6 mm x 2.5 mm centred on the motor shaft, 1-2 mm air gap to the chip CAN SN65HVD230 TX/RX FDCAN1 PA12 (TX) / PA11 (RX); CANH/CANL to the CANable, 120 Ω at both ends Thermistor 10 k NTC on the stator + 10 k to 3.3 V spare ADC input

Check pins against the current Nucleo and IHM07M1 user manuals before powering up; CubeMX may assign alternatives.

docs.title: 6. Bring-up checklist
docs.text:
Follow it in order, and do not raise the supply current limit until a step passes.

  1. Power only, PWM off. 12 V, 0.3 A limit. Board idles, STATUS frames arrive at 100 Hz (run_test.py prints an error if they do not).
  2. Sensors. Turn the rotor by hand: position telemetry follows, one turn = 6.283 rad. Phase currents read about 0 A.
  3. PWM. Scope the three phases at 50 % duty with no motor: 20 kHz, centre-aligned, and the ADC trigger sits in the middle of the low-side-on interval.
  4. Encoder calibration. python host/scripts/calibrate_encoder.py --interface gs_usb --channel 0 --write. Travel must match the pole count, and the offset spread should stay under about 10° electrical.
  5. Current loop. Clamp the rotor, use MODE_CURRENT, step 0.3 A. Compare with sim/figures/01_current_step.png.
  6. Velocity loop. 5 rad/s, then 30 rad/s. compare_sim.py overlays sim and hardware.
  7. Position loop and tracking. Steps, then sine with feedforward.
  8. Faults. Kill the Python script (comms timeout), grab the inertia disk (collision), unplug the encoder while it turns slowly (encoder fault).

docs.title: 7. Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Motor vibrates or locks up in velocity mode wrong encoder offset or direction: rerun calibration ENC_MODEL fault as soon as the motor moves wrong R, L or Kt, wrong pole count, or wrong current-sense gain; identify parameters (system_identification.md) COLLISION trips on fast moves J or friction values off, or threshold too low; check the tau_ext column in the log No STATUS frames bitrate mismatch, missing 120 Ω termination, wrong node id, or the CANable is in slcan mode while gs_usb is selected Currents read a constant offset offset calibration ran with PWM off or the motor moving; restart with the rotor still COMM_TIMEOUT during long tests PC sleeping or the USB adapter dropped; heartbeat runs at 50 Hz, timeout is 50 ms

docs.title: Research paper ideas
docs.text: Ranked by fit with the testbed and the time available (November to February). The simulation results in sim/figures/ are already preliminary evidence for #1 and #2.

docs.title: 1. Model-based fault detection and isolation for joint actuators (strongest; thesis-sized)
docs.text:
Question. Can a joint actuator tell a sensor fault from a mechanical event using only signals the FOC loop already has?

Idea. Two residuals that respond to different things: the back-EMF voltage residual reacts to encoder faults but not to load torque; the momentum observer reacts to external torque but not to encoder faults (while the encoder is healthy). Together they isolate the fault class, then the drive picks the right reaction.

Evidence so far (sim). A silent encoder freeze (no error flag) is caught in 3.3 ms; a collision is caught 0.8 ms after contact with 0.12 Nm peak contact torque, against 30 ms and 0.45 Nm with a following-error check.

Hardware experiments. Encoder unplug / magnet shift / injected freeze, phase open circuit, collisions at several speeds, payload changes. Report detection latency, false-alarm rate over long normal runs (sine, chirp, random moves), and ROC curves versus threshold.

Venues. IEEE/ASME AIM, IEEE IECON, IFAC SAFEPROCESS, IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (with a strong hardware section).

docs.title: 2. Encoder-fault-tolerant control: keep the joint alive instead of stopping
docs.text: Extend #1: on ENC_MODEL, switch to a sensorless back-EMF observer (above a minimum speed) or to a "limp home" torque mode, so a humanoid leg does not drop. Measure the transition transient and how far the joint degrades. This is the natural thesis chapter after #1 and maps directly to humanoid reliability.

docs.title: 3. Data-driven friction and cogging compensation from logged data
docs.text: Use the 1 kHz logs to fit position-dependent cogging plus friction (lookup table, or a small network), feed it forward, and report the tracking-error drop on top of the model feedforward. Easy to execute, good for a workshop or student paper; it also makes the main demo look better.

docs.title: 4. Cross-project: from joint-level faults to cell-level OEE (with the Siemens project)
docs.text: Publish the actuator's fault events and health residuals over OPC UA (Python asyncua server) into the production-cell project, treat the joint as one station of the simulated cell, and quantify how detection latency and fault isolation change availability and OEE. Frame it as a digital-twin / Industry 4.0 health monitoring architecture. Fits IEEE ETFA, CASE or INDIN, which industrial automation teams read.

docs.title: 5. Siemens cell alone (lower priority)
docs.text: A virtual-commissioning workflow (Factory I/O + PLCSIM Advanced + S7-GRAPH + OPC UA dashboard) as a teaching or rapid-prototyping case study, for example for ASEE or an IFAC education workshop. Useful for the CV; less novel as research.

docs.title: Suggested path
docs.text: Write #1 as the main paper (draft by early February, using sim + first hardware results), keep #2 as the thesis extension, and do #4 only if the Siemens project reaches OPC UA by mid-January. Ask an ASU faculty member in controls or robotics early whether they would co-advise; a hardware FDI paper is easier to publish with a faculty co-author.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
All results below are from the simulation (GM4108-class gimbal motor, 24 V bus). Every figure is regenerated by python -m experiments.run_all, and CI fails if a result drifts. Hardware results will be added next to these as the bench comes up.

docs.title: Silent encoder freeze
docs.text: The encoder stops updating without raising any error flag. The back-EMF residual sees that the voltage the motor needs no longer matches the speed the encoder reports.

docs.title: System identification: replacing the placeholder motor numbers
docs.text:
Every gain is derived from MotorParams (sim) / act_default_config (firmware), so identify these once on the bench and paste them into both places.

Parameter Method Tool Pole pairs p Spin by hand, count cogging steps / 2, or the calibration script travel check calibrate_encoder.py Phase resistance R DC current through two phases with the rotor locked: R_phase = V / I / 2. Use 4-wire measurement or the bench supply at low current multimeter Inductance L Locked rotor, MODE_CURRENT step of 0.3 A with a low-gain loop, fit the first-order rise (tau = L/R); or an LCR meter between two phases / 2 run_test.py + fit Electrical offset, direction Open-loop alignment at several electrical angles calibrate_encoder.py --write Kt Lever arm on a scale (or load cell): hold MODE_TORQUE at several iq, Kt = F x r / iq. Cross-check with back-EMF: spin with another motor or by hand, Kt = 1.5 p lambda scale, run_test.py J, b, Tc Torque chirp (--test chirp_torque) and constant-velocity runs: Tc + b w = Kt iq at steady speed (fit a line over 5-50 rad/s); J from the chirp frequency response or from accel/decel slopes chirp_torque log + least squares Thermal R_th, C_th Hold 1.5 A locked for 10 min with the NTC logged, fit a first-order rise NTC channel

After updating the numbers: rerun python -m experiments.run_all and make -C firmware/tests, then compare the hardware step logs against the new sim figures. The size of the gap is a result worth reporting (model fidelity).
